title_en: Homily on the Ascension of Christ
author: Epiphanius of Salamis
addressee: a Christian congregation celebrating the feast of the Ascension
occasion: A festal homily for the Ascension of Christ, explaining why this feast is the crown of the Lord's feasts and answering Jewish objections by comparing Christ's ascension with Elijah's.
argument: The Ascension is the completion and crown of all the feasts of Christ, surpassing his birth, baptism, resurrection, and Pentecost because in it human flesh is exalted to the heavenly throne. Against Jewish objections that Elijah also ascended, Epiphanius argues from Scripture that Elijah was taken up only 'as into heaven,' while Christ alone, who came down from heaven, truly ascended. He dramatizes the devil's defeat through a first-person lament in which the devil recounts his deception, his orchestration of Christ's passion through the Jews, and his repeated failed attempts to defeat Christ, with Psalm verses quoted within the lament and by the narrator to proclaim Christ's universal kingship. Finally, he applies the parable of the sower to the Church as the good soil bearing fruit thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold, and closes with the angels' promise that Christ will return in the same way he ascended.

outline.move: Epiphanius praises the Ascension as the crown of the feasts, asks for the congregation's attentive prayer, and reviews the earlier feasts of Christ's birth, baptism, resurrection, and Pentecost, showing how each was incomplete until today's feast.

He answers Jewish objections that Elijah also ascended by distinguishing 'as into heaven' from 'into heaven,' presents Christ as the good shepherd bringing the lost sheep to the Father, and begins the devil's first-person lament over his defeat.

He continues the devil's lament, in which the devil recounts his deception and failed attempts against Christ, quotes Psalm verses celebrating Christ's ascension, and reflects on the earthquake as a past event in which the earth, personified as a mother interceding for her children, testified that it belongs to the Lord.
He applies the parable of the sower to the Church as good soil, exhorts the congregation to resist the devil, and closes with the angels' words that Christ will return as he ascended.

cast.name: Epiphanius
cast.who: The preacher, bishop of Cyprus, delivering the homily.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The ascended Lord, whose human flesh is exalted to heaven.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: The prophet cited by Jewish opponents as a precedent for ascension.

cast.name: the devil
cast.who: The defeated enemy who laments Christ's victory and ascension.

cast.name: the Jews
cast.who: Opponents who object that Elijah also ascended and who are criticized for misreading Scripture.

cast.name: John
cast.who: The witness at Christ's baptism who proclaimed him the Lamb of God; the source names him only as 'John,' though the context strongly suggests John the Baptist.

cast.name: the Father
cast.who: God the Father, who testifies to the Son and receives the lost sheep.

cast.name: the two men in white
cast.who: The angels at the Ascension who announce Christ's return.

voices.speaker: the devil
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'σήμερον ὁ διάβολος θρηνεῖ λέγων' and continued in first-person lament

voices.speaker: Christ (as shepherd)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'δωροφορῶν φθέγγεται' after a long relative clause describing the shepherd, indicating he speaks while offering the gift to the Father

voices.speaker: the two men in white
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'Τί οὖν οἱ ὀφθέντες ἐκήρυττον;' and quoted directly; the quotation includes multiple sentences of exhortation, beginning with 'Ἄνδρες Ἰσραηλῖται, τί ἑστήκατε βλέποντες εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν;'

key_terms.sense: The Ascension of Christ, the feast being celebrated
Human flesh, especially Christ's human nature exalted to heaven
The feast of Christ's baptism, when the Trinity was manifested
The lost sheep, representing fallen humanity rescued by Christ
A name for the devil, the enemy overthrown by Christ
The Church, the good soil bearing fruit for Christ
Heretical groups that choke the seed of piety
Virginity, the angel-like state bearing sixtyfold fruit
Self-control or chastity, the yoke bearing thirtyfold fruit

scripture: The author quotes the Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering and uses LXX book names. Psalm references should be cited in modern form with LXX numbering noted where it differs from the Hebrew (e.g., LXX Psalm 46 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 47).
uncertain: Whether the homily was delivered in Cyprus or elsewhere
The exact identity of the Jewish interlocutors (whether a real community or a rhetorical construct)
Whether 'John' at the baptism is explicitly John the Baptist or simply 'John' as named in the source

_unresolved_facts.claim: Psalm verses quoted within the lament and by the narrator to proclaim Christ's universal kingship
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Διὸ καὶ Ψαλμῳδὸς ἐκ πολλῶν τῶν χρόνων ἐβόα λέγων· Πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, κροτήσατε χεῖρας· ἀλαλάξατε τῷ Θεῷ ἐν φωνῇ ἀγαλλιάσεως, ὅτι Κύριος ὕψιστος, βασιλεὺς φοβερὸς, μέγας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν· καὶ πάλιν· Ἀνέβη ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἀλαλαγμῷ, Κύριος ἐν φωνῇ σάλπιγγος.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Psalm verses are quoted within the devil's lament, not by a separate narrator. The devil himself quotes the Psalms as part of his speech, expressing his frustration at Christ's victory.

_unresolved_facts.claim: reflects on the earthquake as a past event in which the earth, personified as a mother interceding for her children, testified that it belongs to the Lord
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἡ γὰρ γῆ τὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ὄνομα μὴ φέρουσα ἀκαρτερήτῳ τρόμῳ ἐβράσσετο, διὰ τὴν ἀταξίαν τῶν αὐτῆς τέκνων μαστιζομένη, καθάπερ στόμα κατὰ τῶν στοιχείων ἀνοίξασα ῥήγματα, τῆς κρυπτομένης ὀδύνης ἐβόα τὸ μέγεθος· καὶ φείσασθαι τῶν ἡμαρτηκότων, ὡς μήτηρ ὑπὲρ τέκνων, ἱκέτευε.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The earthquake is presented as a past event (the crucifixion/resurrection), but the earth's personification as a mother interceding is part of the ongoing reflection within the devil's lament, not a separate narrator's reflection. The devil is describing how the earth testified to Christ's lordship.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Christ (as shepherd) ... 'δωροφορῶν φθέγγεται' after a long relative clause describing the shepherd, indicating he speaks while offering the gift to the Father
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός, ὁ τὰ ἐνενήκοντα ἐννέα τῶν ἀγγέλων πρόβατα καταλιπὼν ἐπὶ τὰ οὐράνια ὄρη, καὶ τὸ πεπλανημένον πρόβατον εὑρηκὼς, καὶ ὤμοις φιλανθρωπίας βαστάζων, καὶ εἰς τὸν οὐράνιον λιμένα ἀνενεγκὼν, τῷ ἰδίῳ Γεννήτορι δωροφορῶν φθέγγεται· Εὗρον, Πάτερ, τὸ πρόβατον τὸ πλανώμενον...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The relative clause describes Christ as shepherd, but 'δωροφορῶν φθέγγεται' is third-person narration about Christ, not a marker of direct speech by Christ. The first-person speech 'Εὗρον, Πάτερ...' is Christ speaking, but the brief overstates the grammatical marking. The phrase indicates 'bearing it as a gift, he says/speaks'—the participle δωροφορῶν goes with the subject of the relative clause (Christ), but the construction is more complex than simple direct speech introduction.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the devil ... source_forms include 'ὁ ἄθλιος', 'ὁ τάλας'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τί ποιήσω, ὁ ἄθλιος; ... Τί ποιήσω ὁ τάλας;
_unresolved_facts.fix: These are not source forms identifying the devil by name/epithet in third person; they are first-person self-addresses within the devil's speech ('What shall I do, wretched one?' / 'What shall I do, miserable one?'). They function as the devil speaking about himself in first person, not as third-person identifiers.

The brief omits 'οἱ βάσκανοι' (the envious/malignant ones), which is part of the epithet. The full form is 'Ἰουδαίων παῖδες οἱ βάσκανοι'—'the envious children of the Jews' or 'the malignant Jewish children.'
